notes.h: Why fabric care depends on fibre type
notes.b: A garment's care label is not arbitrary: a fabric's properties come from its fibres, its yarn and its construction, and these decide how it reacts to water, heat, friction and detergent. Knowing the fibre family tells you how to wash, dry and iron it safely.
points: Natural cellulose fibres (cotton, linen) absorb water readily, swell when wet and are strong when wet, so they can be washed hot and often. They also crease easily and tend to shrink on first washing.

Protein fibres (wool, silk) absorb moisture but are damaged by alkaline detergents and high temperatures, so they need a mild or wool-specific detergent, a low temperature and gentle action. Wool is washed cool, about 30 °C, as the label states.
Wool can felt or shrink when agitated in hot water, which is why hot, rough washing ruins it.

Manufactured fibres such as polyester and nylon absorb very little water, dry quickly, keep their shape and resist creasing. They can attract static, and they melt or glaze under a hot iron or high tumble-dry heat.

Blended fabrics combine the care needs of both fibres, so the more sensitive (most delicate) fibre sets the washing temperature and ironing heat. For example, a wool/polyester mixture is washed and ironed as wool.

Fabric construction matters too: a tightly woven fabric resists water and wind more than a loosely knitted one, because the gaps between yarns are smaller. Knitted fabric stretches and can sag or shrink.
notes.tip: If asked why a property matters for care, link it to the use: crease resistant means easier washing and ironing, strong when wet means it can be washed often without stretching or tearing, and colour-fast means the colour does not run or fade.

notes.b: Shrinkage is a permanent reduction in a fabric's length or width after laundering. It happens in three different ways, and the cause decides how to prevent it.
points: Relaxation shrinkage happens because fibres stretched during spinning, weaving and finishing relax back to their natural length in water. It is most marked in cotton, linen and viscose.
Felting shrinkage happens to wool when the scales on its fibres interlock under heat, moisture and agitation. The fabric thickens and shrinks, and this cannot be reversed.
Heat shrinkage occurs when a fabric is washed or tumble dried hotter than it can tolerate, especially in knitted and thermoplastic fabrics (those that soften with heat).
Percentage shrinkage = (original length − new length) ÷ original length × 100.
Prevention: follow the care label, wash at the stated temperature and avoid hot tumble drying, because heat is a common cause.
Pre-shrunk fabric or a shrink-resistant finish reduces shrinkage in garments that will be laundered often. Washing a test sample of fabric before cutting out a garment shows how much it will shrink.
notes.tip: Don't mix up the causes: felting is the shrinkage of wool, while relaxation shrinkage is mainly in cellulose fibres. Both are irreversible but have different causes.

notes.b: Water repellence is how well a fabric resists wetting. It matters for rainwear and for choosing the right fabric for a garment.
points: Three things give a fabric water repellence: a close weave or tight knit, so the gaps between yarns are too small for water to penetrate; a fibre that absorbs little water; and a water-repellent finish.
Fibres that do not absorb water, such as polyester and nylon, shed water more readily than cotton or linen. Cotton and wool absorb water, so they are not naturally repellent.
A water-repellent finish coats the surface of the fabric with a chemical so that water forms beads that roll off.
Washing and wear reduce a finish, so a repellent garment may need re-proofing.
Water-repellent (showerproof) fabric resists wetting but will let water through in heavy or prolonged rain.
A waterproof fabric (coated or laminated, with sealed seams) stops water passing through entirely.
Breathable fabrics let perspiration vapour escape while keeping rain out, so the wearer stays dry inside as well as outside.
notes.tip: Water-repellent is not the same as waterproof, and breathable is not the same as water-repellent. Keep the three terms separate in your answer.

notes.b: Crease recovery is how well a fabric springs back to its smooth state after being folded or crushed. It decides how much ironing a garment needs.
points: A crease forms when fibres are bent and the bonds between them shift, holding the fabric in the folded position.

Cotton, linen and viscose have poor recovery, so they crease easily and need ironing. In cotton and linen, cellulose chains form hydrogen bonds that break and re-form when the fabric is wet and dried.
Wool recovers well because its fibres are elastic, and creases hang out or can be relaxed by steaming.
Polyester and nylon have good crease recovery because their fibres spring back to shape once the folding force is removed.
Crease-resistant finishes, such as resin finishes on cotton or linen, improve recovery and cut down ironing. Blending with polyester also helps.
Care link: damp garments can be shaken and hung to reduce creases, and ironing temperature must match the fibre.
notes.tip: Questions on why crease resistance matters want the practical benefit: easier washing and ironing, and less creasing when worn.

notes.b: Care labels use a fixed set of symbols so that anyone can read how to launder a garment safely, whatever language the label is in. Reading the label before buying and before washing helps you avoid shrinkage, colour loss and damage.
points: The symbols are international (standard ISO 3758; GINETEX is the European association behind them) and appear in a fixed order: washing, bleaching, drying, ironing, then professional care.
Wash: a washtub means the garment may be machine washed, and the number or dots in the tub give the maximum water temperature. Bars under the tub mean gentler action.
A hand in the tub means hand wash only, usually at a low temperature with gentle action. A cross over the tub means do not wash in water.
Bleach: a triangle means bleach may be used; a crossed-out triangle means do not bleach.
Drying: a square containing a circle means tumble drying is allowed, with dots showing the heat setting; a crossed tumble-dry symbol means do not tumble dry.
A square with a horizontal line means dry flat; a square with one vertical line means line dry. Drip dry means hang the wet garment to drip without wringing.
Iron: one dot means a cool (low) iron, two dots a warm or medium iron and three dots a hot iron; a crossed iron means do not iron.
Dry cleaning: a circle shows dry cleaning is allowed, and the letters inside tell the cleaner which solvent process to use. A crossed circle means do not dry clean.
Diagram: draw and label the washtub (with 30 or 40 or dots), hand wash, triangle with a cross, tumble dry, dry flat, iron with two dots, and circle (dry clean).
notes.tip: Ordinary Level asks you to state what two shown symbols tell the consumer, for example hand wash only with do not bleach, or drip dry with do not tumble dry. Give the plain meaning in a few words, with the reason where useful (for example wool or delicates).

notes.h: Detergent components and how they clean
notes.b: A modern laundry detergent contains several components, each with a specific job in removing soil from the fabric. Choosing a detergent to match the fabric depends on knowing what each does.
points: Surfactants reduce the surface tension of water, so the water can wet the fibres thoroughly. One end of a surfactant molecule attracts water and the other attracts oil and grease, so they lift oily and greasy soil away and break it into small particles.
Surfactants hold the loosened soil suspended in the wash water, so it is rinsed away and does not redeposit on the fabric.

Enzymes (in biological detergents) are proteins that act as biological catalysts, speeding up the breakdown of stains: protease breaks down protein stains such as blood and egg, amylase breaks down starch stains and lipase breaks down fat stains.
Enzymes work best in warm, not hot, water and are damaged or destroyed by very high temperatures.
Fluorescent whitening agents (optical brighteners) absorb ultraviolet light and re-emit it as blue-white light, which makes white and light fabrics look brighter and whiter.
Fluorescent agents do not clean or remove stains; they only change how the fabric reflects light.
Match the detergent to the fabric: use a mild detergent for wool and silk. A biological detergent is not for wool or silk, because enzymes can attack their protein fibres.
notes.tip: Candidates often swap these three. Surfactants lift soil, enzymes digest stains, and fluorescents only change appearance. Higher Level has asked for the purpose of two of them.

notes.b: Simple tests let you compare how different fabrics behave, using their general properties of shrinkage, water repellence and crease recovery. They only give useful results if the test is fair.
points: Shrinkage test: mark and measure a square on each sample, wash and dry under identical conditions, remeasure and calculate the percentage shrinkage.
Water-repellence test: place drops of water on each sample (flat or on a slope) and time or observe whether the drops bead and roll off, or soak in and darken the fabric.
Crease-recovery test: crumple equal-sized samples in a closed fist for one minute, release, and compare how smooth each is after a set time.
Fair test: use equal-sized samples, the same conditions and the same timing, so that the only variable is the fabric. Name the fibre or fabric of each sample.
Repeat the test on several samples of each fabric to give reliable results, note any variation, and record the results in a table.
Draw a conclusion on how suitable each fabric is for a garment, using your results.
notes.tip: For a procedure answer, state equal samples, the same conditions and a comparison of results. Coursework expects a fair-test method, percentage shrinkage and a conclusion on suitability for a garment.

keyTerms.definition: The reduction in a fabric's length or width caused by laundering, drying or heat.
The irreversible matting of wool fibres caused by heat, moisture and agitation, as their scales interlock.
The ability of a fabric to stop water wetting or passing through it, through its structure or a surface finish.
The ability of a fabric to return to its smooth state after being folded or crushed.
A detergent component that reduces the surface tension of water so that it can wet fibres and lift soil away.
A biological catalyst in a detergent that breaks down specific stains such as protein, starch or fat.
A detergent component that absorbs ultraviolet light and emits blue light, making white fabric appear whiter.
A fabric that allows water vapour from perspiration to pass out while still resisting rain.

factCards.term: Three fibre types with the most water absorbency
factCards.definition: Cotton, linen and wool absorb water readily; polyester and nylon absorb very little.
Relaxation shrinkage in cotton and linen, felting shrinkage in wool, and heat shrinkage from over-hot washing or tumble drying.

factCards.term: Three enzymes in laundry detergent and the stains they break down
factCards.definition: Proteases break down protein stains, amylases break down starch stains and lipases break down fat stains.

factCards.term: Three ways to reduce shrinkage in a garment
factCards.definition: Wash at a suitable temperature, avoid tumble drying, and buy pre-shrunk or shrink-proofed fabric.
A triangle with diagonal stripes or a cross through it; bleach must not be used on the fabric.
A washtub with a hand inside it, usually at low temperature with gentle action.
An iron with two dots, suitable for wool and wool-polyester blends.

factCards.term: Two ways to improve crease recovery
factCards.definition: Applying a resin crease-resistant finish to cotton or linen, and steaming to relax wrinkles in wool.

questions.prompt: Explain what happens to a cotton shirt in a hot wash that is then tumble dried, and name the type of shrinkage involved.
questions.model: Cotton is a cellulose fibre, and its fibres release the tension set during spinning and weaving when wet, so they return to a shorter, looser length. The hot water speeds this relaxation, and tumble drying applies further heat that shortens the fabric. The result is relaxation shrinkage combined with heat shrinkage, which reduces the garment's length and width and can make it tight to wear. Washing at a lower temperature and drying flat or on a line reduces the problem.

questions.prompt: Describe how a detergent removes a greasy stain from a cotton garment, referring to at least three detergent components and the care needed for fabric and colour.
questions.model: Surfactants reduce the surface tension of the wash water, so it can wet the cotton fibres and penetrate beneath the greasy soil, lifting it away from the fabric. The surfactant molecules surround the loosened grease and keep it suspended in the water, so it does not redeposit on the garment. Lipases, an enzyme, break down fat stains into smaller molecules that wash out more easily, and they work best within a suitable temperature range. Fluorescent whitening agents do not remove stains; they only make white fabric look brighter and should be avoided on coloured fabrics. Care is needed to choose a wash temperature that suits the fabric and the enzymes, to check the care label for bleach and drying instructions, and to separate colours so that dye does not run. Pre-treating a stain before washing improves the result.
